label: Conan and Taurus cooperate in the attempted theft of the Elephant's Heart.
continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)

citations.locator: Chapter II, paragraphs beginning “By Bel, god of thieves” through Taurus's death in the upper chamber

label: Conan infiltrates Yara's tower and brings Yag-kosha's final enchantment to Yara.
continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)

citations.locator: Chapter I, tower-entry sequence; Chapter III, paragraphs beginning “Yara!” through the jewel's disappearance
supports: Conan seeks Yara's jewel, confronts Yara, and delivers the requested final enchantment.

note: Direction records Conan's action against Yara in this one story.

label: Yag-kosha says that Yara first learned wisdom from him before enslaving him.
continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)

citations.locator: Chapter III, Yag-kosha's account, paragraphs beginning “First he sat at my feet” and “But his wisdom was deeper”
supports: Yag-kosha recounts Yara's earlier learning and subsequent betrayal.

note: This pre-story relation is Yag-kosha's testimony, not independently corroborated outside the tale.

label: Yara enslaves and tortures Yag-kosha in Yag-kosha's account; the final enchantment turns that conflict against Yara.
continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)

citations.locator: Chapter III, Yag-kosha's account of captivity; final jewel-working sequence
supports: Yag-kosha describes Yara's enslavement and torture, and the story narrates the resulting enchantment's effect on Yara.

note: The captivity history is Yag-kosha's testimony; the ending is directly narrated.

label: Yag-kosha asks Conan to perform the Blood-and-Jewel working that releases him and reaches Yara.
continuity: Robert E. Howard, “The Tower of the Elephant” (Weird Tales, March 1933)

citations.locator: Chapter III, paragraphs beginning “For I feel the end of time draw near” through “Take your sword”

note: ‘Other’ preserves this specific requested ritual assistance without forcing it into a generic patron/created/transformed relation.
